email.scenario: You hold a season subscription at a small local theater and have enjoyed this season's plays from the same seat. The theater recently renovated its auditorium, and at the last performance you discovered that your seat now sits directly behind a new support pillar that blocks half of the stage. The next play is two weeks away. Write an email to the theater's subscriptions coordinator, whom you have never met.
email.subject: Season subscription seat with a blocked view
bullets: Express your appreciation for the plays the theater has staged this season.
Describe how the new pillar blocks the view of the stage from your assigned seat.
Request an exchange to a different seat, such as an aisle seat, for the remaining performances.

academicDiscussion.professorPost: This week we are looking at how daily schedules affect teenagers' rest. Some school districts have proposed that secondary schools begin the day an hour later so that students can sleep longer. Because lessons would then also finish an hour later, sports practice, clubs, and part-time jobs would be pushed further into the evening, and families would have to adjust their morning routines. What do you think? Should secondary schools start an hour later? Why or why not?

studentPosts.name: Mirela
studentPosts.post: I support the later start. Most teenagers I know cannot fall asleep early even when they try, so they sit through first period half awake and remember very little of it. An extra hour of sleep would make morning lessons actually useful, and that matters more than finishing the day a bit earlier.

studentPosts.name: Tobias
studentPosts.post: I disagree. If school ends an hour later, team practice and club meetings run into the evening, and students with part-time jobs lose a shift. Many parents also leave for work early and could no longer drop their children off. I suspect teenagers would simply go to bed later and gain nothing.
